utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What about the situation in Prijedor? Were you well acquainted with the situation in Prijedor? Would an action of this kind be a dangerous one in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. Each case is a separate case. As far as I know, Prijedor, perhaps it would be, but perhaps not. You have to know individual people in order to be able to state an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What about Mr. Vila? Did he show any fear? Was he afraid of employing in Prijedor two Muslim electricians?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vila did show a certain amount of fear in employing those two men, whereas the person wearing the uniform - as I learnt later on, I learnt that the man in uniform was Miroslav Kvocka - he insisted and tried to persuade Mr. Ranko Vila to give jobs to those two men, to give them some work to do so that they could earn enough money to survive, to earn a livelihood. He insisted upon saying that they were very good electricians and that they were ready to do hard work in order to earn some money.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did they go their own ways there? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how long they were there for. Mr. Vila went back to the offices; Mr. Miroslav Kvocka, he left on his bicycle, he left the compound of that particular factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You saw Mr. Kvocka for the first time on that occasion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's true that I saw him for the first time. But I knew him from the times I worked; that is to say, I knew him from meetings in different regions. The Prijedor region belonged to Banja Luka. And we knew each other by sight, actually. We weren't close.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: But when he came, you didn't know -- when he arrived, you didn't know that he was Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was only through the conversation that he had with Mr. Vila that I came to realise that the man was Miroslav Kvocka. And I let it be known that we knew each other from before, when I was a policeman in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So you only knew him by sight; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Yes, only by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you happen to know whether the men got the jobs or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: I don't know. That was the last time that I transported goods to Mr. Ranko Vila's firm. I didn't go there anymore so I don't know. I have no idea whether those two men were employed or not. I really don't know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, an agreement was not reached as to whether they would be accepted or not.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vila did agree. After this lengthy conversation, he agreed to have those workers brought in, the two young men, but that the other man should guarantee -- be a guarantee for them and that he should ensure that it was those two particular men who were going to work. So he did succeed in convincing Mr. Vila to take the two men on. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Krstan Simic. I see that it is Mr. Saxon. Oh, I do beg your pardon. What about the other Defence teams? Anybody else who would like to ask this witness a question? I do not see anybody on their feet so I think it is up to Mr. Saxon. Mr. Saxon, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Racic, can you explain why you had such high expenses before you finally left the police force?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Well, I like living well, and of course you cannot do that on a police salary. I like to live well and that's why I had high expenses, and I was looking for side jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you have a problem with alcohol or drug abuse?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: No. Quite the contrary. I don't drink and I don't use drugs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you have a problem with gambling?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How many years altogether were you in the police force in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: I worked in the police from the 1st of January, 1980 until the 10th of February, 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why, then, if you like to live well and you could not do that as a police officer, did you remain in the police force for seven years?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: In the police, working in the police in that period, it was possible to have your housing situation resolved, and just at the moment when I was about to get a flat, I was sacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So in other words, the remuneration as a police officer was not so bad, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: On a police salary, you could live normally for quite a few years. We had to be a subtenant somewhere for about ten years before you could get your own flat. I come from a poor family. I always liked to have a good car and that's why I pursued other activities. I worked as a car mechanic, repaired cars. And I don't think I was mistaken or that I did anything wrong that -- doing those side jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. Moving on to another topic. If I understood your testimony correctly, you explained that the head of the police station is a commander. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then there will be a deputy commander in that police station, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then depending on the number of subsections within that police station and the size of the station, there might be an assistant commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Assistant commander could or could not be -- would not be there, depending on the size of the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. To summarise: The bigger the police station, the more likelihood there would be a commander, a deputy commander, and an assistant commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, during your seven-year tenure in the police department, did the Banja Luka police department ever have to take care of, for example, 3.000 prisoners at one time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: The question is not very clear to me. Just a minute. In my time, there was never 3.000 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If a police station had to take care of, shall we say, 3.000 prisoners, would you agree with me that that police station would probably -- MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] My learned colleague is asking this witness to make suppositions. The police station is regulated by the Rules of Service and what everyone is doing is strictly regulated by the rules, and looking for such an answer for a regular policeman is improper, I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall hear the witness answer in any case. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will finish my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: ... the police station had to take care of, shall we say, 3.000 prisoners, would you agree with me that that police station would probably be big enough to have a commander, a deputy commander, and an assistant commander?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Well, with regard to 3.000 prisoners, I cannot give you a definitive answer. It's something that has to be decided from a higher level. It's a special situation, 3.000 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on. You mentioned the conversation that you overheard between Mr. Kvocka and the man known as Ranko Vila that concerned the possible employment of two young Muslim men, and you described how finally, after some discussion, Mr. Ranko Vila finally agreed to employ these two young men if Mr. Kvocka would act as a guarantee. Have I summarised your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ranko Vila was saying that he needs electricians, people of that occupation, but he was nervous about employing Muslims. And Mr. Kvocka was interceding with Mr. Vila, saying that in his spare time he would be present there and, if necessary, work as an assistant to those workers. But he was begging him to employ these two people in order to help them survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Approximately when did this conversation occur?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "at what time."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you give me a year, perhaps a month?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The year was 1994. It was in the summer. It could have been June, July, or August. I cannot say that exactly, a lot of time has passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So then Mr. Ranko Vila decided to trust Mr. Kvocka at that time, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Yes. He decided to help Mr. Kvocka and to employ these two people with certain guarantees of security on his part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, with your knowledge of police procedures, wouldn't it have been a violation of proper police procedures for Mr. Kvocka to make an agreement to also be working outside of his police employment and providing protection, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time when I was working, that was prohibited, but in 1994, it was not a regular situation. It was out of the ordinary. And I don't know whether it was forbidden at that time. Everybody was doing all they could to survive. Those were hard times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Racic, do you know the ethnicity of Mr. Ranko Vila?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. Judging by his first and last names, I think he should be of Orthodox faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Does that mean a Serb, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I understand the line of employment that you went into after you left the police force, you hauled property in trucks or in a large truck; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever haul property that had been taken from the homes of Muslims or Croats who were forced to leave Prijedor or Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: No. I had a small truck, carrying up to 4 tonnes, and I could provide small services, for instance, haul tyres, in case I had a problem on the road. And I had assistant for liquid cargo and for foodstuffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Racic, were you ever present in either the Omarska, Keraterm, or Trnopolje camps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I have the Court's indulgence for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I realise that you were no longer in the police force in 1992, but as a civilian during that time, were you aware of the existence of detention camps for non-Serbs in the Prijedor or the Banja Luka area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: I was aware of that from what I learned from the media, to the extent we could find out about that from the radio, television, et cetera, because sometimes there was no electricity. Since I was a driver, I had a radio in my truck, and I knew from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were you aware that the persons detained in these camps had been pushed from their homes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Well, I could suppose that if a person was in a camp, he must have had a house in that area, but I was not an eyewitness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the media at that time explain why these people were in these detention camps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember that there were any explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Krstan Simic, do you have any redirect? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Racic, when you spoke to my learned colleague about guarantees, were those guarantees of a policeman or of a man who would just be present, something like, "If anything happens, I'm here."

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: It was more of the latter case. "If anything happens, I'm here; it will happen to me as well." MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. Judge Riad, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Racic, good morning. I just would like to have some precision, and perhaps you are in a condition to give it to me. Now, the conversation you witnessed between Mr. Kvocka and Ranko Vila concerned two specific men. It even ended by the fact that Ranko Vila insisted that these two men only will be working there, that they would not be replaced by anyone else. Then who were these two men, if you know, who pushed Mr. Kvocka to, as you said, demean himself and even to suggest that he will come himself to support them and to guarantee them and to work for them? Who were they? Something very special. They're not just two Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: I don't know who they were, those two Muslim men. I don't remember mentioning humiliation. The man was simply willing to offer his support and help in those times, which were really hard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said he would be an auxiliary worker, that is the translation, and he put himself in a demeaning position, so not my words. This is something you would do for a very close person; you'd do it for your father, for your son. Do you know who these two men were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Well, I already told you, I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Also, something else perhaps you know, although your answer was vague. When you were asked what were the consequences for Serbs employing Muslims in Prijedor, what were the consequences, you said, "You have to know individual people in order to be able to state an opinion." But when you speak of the consequences of a society, what would be the consequences at that time in Prijedor if someone employed Muslims in the community? Was it tolerant?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Well, I will state my personal opinion. Be it Prijedor, Sarajevo, or anywhere else, everywhere there were problems. Whether a specific person would experience those problems depended on the situation at hand, on the specific case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Judge Wald, no questions? Mr. Racic, I have a couple of questions. You mentioned that, at that time, people had no means of livelihood. What time are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the time of war. Even today, the situation down there is difficult. I, for instance, have five trucks and it happens sometimes that I don't use a single truck in a month and don't have a single engagement in a month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You answered a question of the Prosecutor that this conversation took place somewhere in August 1994. Is that the same time you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, 1994 was the time of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. My next question. You said, and I quote, "I found out later that that man was Miroslav Kvocka." When did you learn that? After what?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: During the conversation between Mr. Vila and Miroslav Kvocka, I found out from that conversation that the man in the uniform who arrived on a bicycle was Miroslav Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So did Ranko Vila ever mention the name of his collocutor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he used his first or last name. But I did hear that his last name was Kvocka and his first name was Miroslav.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry I have to insist, but we have to be precise. So, finally, how did you find out his name was Kvocka? You knew that man by sight. But how did you find out the name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: From the conversation. The man was addressed by Ranko Vila by his name. Mr. Ranko Vila, when talking to the man, was saying either his first or his last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. Another question. How did you know that these two men were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: Muslim names were mentioned, and they were talking about very good professionals in this business, very good electricians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Racic. Thank you for appearing before the Tribunal. You have completed your testimony. I'm sorry. Judge Riad wants to ask something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You just mentioned that the names of the two young men were mentioned, two Muslim names. Do you remember these names as you remember the name of Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RACIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember those names. I already said I knew Miroslav Kvocka by sight and I knew that there was a man by that name working in the Prijedor region. You must realise that when you see a man in uniform, in a specific situation, you can recall his name; whereas those two other names were a different case, I didn't remember them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I realise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. Thank you very much. We wish you a safe trip to your domicile. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. According to today's schedule, the Defence calls witness Brane Bolta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Bolta. Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take your solemn oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down. Please come closer to the microphone. Are you comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well. Thank you. You will answer now the questions put to you by Mr. Krstan Simic, and then we shall see who will continue. Mr. Krstan Simic, you have the floor. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bolta. Together with Mr. Lukic, I am representing Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I will ask you a series of questions regarding the area of Prijedor and the events which occurred there. Before we begin, for the record, will you please state your first and last names.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Brane Bolta.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Just a little quieter, please. Mr. Bolta, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: 4th of April, 1960.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Ahmetovci, Bosanski Novi municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You're residing where today?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: In The Hague. I mean, in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are you employed?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: In the Public Security Centre Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In that Public Security Centre Prijedor, is there any lower organisational unit where you work?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: There is a traffic police station where I'm working now.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I have a small doubt here. In your pre-trial motion, you mentioned also a man named "Ranko Bolta." I see the last name is "Bolta" and what is written here is "Bolta" -- "Balta," sorry. It's on page 13. What is the name really? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Those were errors we have already straightened out with the Prosecution. The name is Branko Bolta. I'm sorry. This is my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where did you graduate from school?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I graduated from secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Which school?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: A vocational school.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I went to Zagreb to a training course for policemen, lasting for a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When did you graduate; which year? Just a minute. I must ask you, when you hear my question, make a pause for my question to be interpreted and only then answer, to keep the record straight. In what year did you attend this school in Pula?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: From September 1982 to May 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You completed the course. Did you start working in the police?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: In Zagreb, and then I moved to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When did you move to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: At the end of 1983. The 1st of January, 1984, I began working in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What were your work posts from 1984 onwards?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: In 1984, I started working in the police station in Prijedor as a foot policeman and as the junior on-duty officer. Then in May 1984, I was transferred to the police station department in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you started working in Kozarac, who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Mr. Didovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: No, in 1985.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Oh, Milutin Bujic was the commander of the police department.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How many policemen did this Kozarac department have? It's a large community?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes, it is. There were nine policemen, and the commander was the tenth in that police department.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In the Kozarac Police Station department, was there a person with the position of deputy commander to Mr. Bujic?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No. A police station department does not have a deputy commander, it only has a commander. A police station may have a commander, a deputy commander, and two or three assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: A moment ago, you mentioned a person called Osme Didovic. Who is he?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: He is the commander from 1990 onwards, when the changes occurred within the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Does that mean that from the 1st of January, 1990, the commander of the police station department in Kozarac was Osme Didovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did he replace Mr. Milutin Bujic?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did Mr. Didovic have a deputy?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: He did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How long did you continue working in the Kozarac Police Station department?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Until March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Why did you stop working in the police station department in Kozarac in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I stopped working because there was heightened ethnic tensions in Kozarac, and I could no longer work there because there were nationalists and extremists and I was no longer acceptable in the police station department. Then there were the Green Berets who could be seen moving around Kozarac and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: On that -- at that time - we're talking about March 1992 - was your safety and security at risk as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I didn't feel at ease, because the Commander Didovic told me on one occasion, "Mr. Bolta, would you like to go and work in Prijedor?" And I said, "When I consider myself to be at risk, I will myself apply to go to Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Let me ask you again to wait a few seconds after my question before giving your answer. Did I understand you correctly when you said that Mr. Osme Didovic, the Department Commander of the police station department in Kozarac, was conscious of certain extraordinary circumstances when he himself made this suggestion to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So in March 1992, you definitively left Kozarac. Who did you report to, on whose approval, and so on? Tell us briefly, how did this happen?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I reported to the Prijedor Police Station, to the commander, Milutin Cadjo, and he told me I should stay on and work in the Prijedor Police Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: On that occasion, were you given your assignments?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What were they?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I was a foot policeman in a particular area, and I also acted as a duty -- junior on-duty police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, what does that mean, foot patrol service? Could you explain briefly what you do when you have such an assignment?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: A police officer who engages in this activity covers a particular area in the region. So it is his responsibility to ensure safety in the area, to combat crime, ensure law and order, traffic safety, and to monitor persons of interest from the standpoint of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you perform those duties on foot or by car?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: On foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: A person covering such a precinct, does he have any kind of superior rank?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No, there's no rank, a simple policeman, foot policeman, or a policeman acting as a patrol officer. So he's simply a policeman and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, were you ever subject to disciplinary action in the course of your career?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, after the signing of the Dayton Peace Accords and the reforms carried out within the police force of Republika Srpska under the supervision of the International Community, that is, the IPTF, the international police, did you apply for permission to continue working in the police?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Did I submit a request?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In 1995 to continue working as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I did not submit any request. This is only normal. I used to be a policeman and I continued being a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did the IPTF and the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska, did they issue a certificate saying that, in view of the events that had taken place, that you could continue being a policeman?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Does that mean, in the police of Republika Srpska, that the people who remained in the police force fulfil the requirements set by the IPTF in terms of the reforms that are carried out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that Mr. Krstan Simic is testifying instead of the witness, but let us hear you, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, that was going to be part of my objection, Your Honour. At the same time, we have heard no evidence that this witness is qualified to draw such a conclusion or state such an opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, go ahead. I want to say to the parties that I should like to adopt a different procedure. We are wasting a lot of time on objections. As you know, the Chamber has discretionary powers and the Chamber is going to use those powers; otherwise, this will go on forever. So please rephrase your question. You know very well that you were leading. So please proceed. Are you aware of that? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I do admit it, and I will stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Continue. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, did IPTF, in any sense, object or find anything to reproach you for in your prior activities?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Let us now go back to the year 1992. As a policeman of the Prijedor Police Station, as part of the Security Centre, was it known that in the territory of Prijedor municipality there were prisoner camps?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What camps were you aware of that existed?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I knew that there were the Omarska and Keraterm camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Within the framework of your duties and instructions from superiors, did you go to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was your assignment linked to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: My assignment was to transport certain persons who had been sentenced on the basis of state or public security problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who would give you the instructions to transport suspects to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I received orders from my superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When transporting these persons, what did you use?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I used an official car, the brand being Citroen, known as the Black Meraja.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When we mention this car, which we refer to as Marica or Black Meraja, how was it designed? Did it have a separate part for suspects which are being transported?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes, it was a separate section. In the front, there was the driver, co-driver, and possibly two or three policemen, whereas the walled-off area contained the persons being transported.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know how much room there was? For how many people was there room in that part of the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: The vehicle was envisaged to accommodate eight persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Sitting in one row or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: In two rows or, rather, two times four seats on each side of the van.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, was there any rule regulating the transport of suspects? Where did they have to be accommodated?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: According to the Rules of Service in public security, there are strict rules that when people are taken into custody, they have to be boarded in the back part of the van. Should they be behind the driver or co-driver, the person could attack the driver and provoke a traffic accident. Therefore, this was strictly prescribed by the Rules of Service, that all suspects had to be transported in the back of the van.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So we come back to the front part of the van. How many people can fit into the front part?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: The driver, the co-driver, and two to three policemen. It depended.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: My question was: How many people could physically fit into the area in front?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Five. Five persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So would they be sitting in one row or several rows?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: In front, there was the driver and co-driver, and behind their backs, there were seats for three more policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, you mentioned the fact that, following orders from your superiors, you transported suspects to the Omarska camp. Do you know how many times you did that during the period of existence of the camp?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Nusret Sivac?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who is Nusret Sivac?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Nusret Sivac was also employed in the public security station, working on the telephone exchange. If somebody called somebody, he would establish connections through the exchange. So, in fact, he was a policeman working on the telephone exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, in the police, we have an ordinary telephone exchange. But was there some other system of communications, encrypted and confidential communications?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: There was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was Mr. Nusret Sivac working on those means of communication?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you remember when Mr. Nusret Sivac left the police in Prijedor, and do you know why he did that?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I don't know when he left the police in Prijedor and I don't know the reason. But I know that he started working as a cameraman for TV Sarajevo, that is, for its studio in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: During one of your transports to Omarska, was Mr. Nusret Sivac among the people you transported and whom you knew, as you just said?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you do that on your own?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who was with you among the policemen?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Policeman Tomo Stojakovic and Dragan Bosancic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were they active-duty or reserve policemen?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Tomo Stojakovic was an active-duty policeman, whereas Bosancic was a reserve policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Talking about the reserve police force, those reserve policemen, while being engaged as part of the police, did they receive any remuneration or salary?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was there any difference in salary between active-duty and reserve officers?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes. They had lower salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How much lower?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Well, they were treated as beginners.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So the reserve policemen would have the lowest salary within the range of salaries for police officers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Tomo Stojakovic, is he alive?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: And this reserve police officer that you mentioned, is he?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you remember the occasion when you were transporting Mr. Nusret Sivac to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I think that this occurred in 1992, between the 8th and the 12th of June. I can't remember the exact date. But in any event, it was in June, between the 8th and the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where did you pick Mr. Sivac from? Where did you set out from?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: The starting point was the Public Security Station Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was Mr. Sivac alone or were there other persons with him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: There were two other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where did you put them in the police van?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: As I have already said, in the back part of the van, the part that was separated from the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Let us make it quite clear: Is that the area that is prescribed by regulations for the transport of suspects, persons taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: On that occasion, were you instructed by your superiors to transport some persons from Keraterm to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes. There was two-way transport. So we were told to stop off at the Keraterm camp as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who did you report to when you arrived at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: As soon as we had arrived, the persons had been prepared for transport. So there were people who were on duty in front of the actual entrance to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you notify anyone that you were coming to pick up those men?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No, I did not. I was just given the assignment to transport them.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How many persons were picked up in Keraterm and transported to Omarska; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I think there were five persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When I say "you," I mean your whole team. Did you have a description of the persons that you were taking to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Let me go back to this police van. Who was driving the van?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who was sitting next to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Tomo Stojakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: And where was the reserve police officer sitting?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Whose duty was it to have the list with the names of people that were being transported?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Policeman Tomo Stojakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you reached Omarska, where did you stop?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I stopped within the Omarska complex, that is, at the corner of the administrative building that existed in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did any of you get out of the van?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: When I came to a halt, Tomo Stojakovic got off the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who opened the back door where the suspects were?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Policeman Tomo Stojakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did those persons get off?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, did anyone approach you then?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes, a reserve policeman who was at the entrance to Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you say a "reserve policeman," how could you distinguish between an active-duty and a reserve policeman?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: A reserve policeman had different uniforms. They were issued these uniforms when they joined, whereas regular policemen had the prescribed uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: These cloth uniforms, were they blue in colour?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So the difference appears to be only in the thickness of the material but the colour was the same?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, please be careful. The witness never mentioned blue cloth. You are testifying for him. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. Maybe the translation omitted to say it. The witness did explicitly say that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this was a woollen cloth uniform. I just wanted to avoid any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sorry. But go ahead, please. Maybe it was a problem of translation. I heard the "woollen cloth" the second time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. They did not recognise the word when the witness used it the first time. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, what was the person doing from the reserve police force, and did that person have any contact with any one of you?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: He came up to Tomo Stojakovic, who -- came up to Tomo Stojakovic when the persons we were transporting got off.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did Tomo Stojakovic give him anything on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes. He gave him the list with the names of those persons on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Just then did some other persons come up to you who took over the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes. Some people who were there in Omarska, they were dressed in a special way, they had special uniforms, they took over those persons and they searched them.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were those persons members of the reserve force of the Omarska Police Station department?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: They were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: But do you know who they were?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I later learnt that they were a special unit from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You said that they were members of a special unit from Banja Luka and that they started searching those persons. How did they do that?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: They did not act strictly in accordance with the rules regulating public security. They did it in a rough and insolent way. The persons were lined up against the wall with their hands spread, with three fingers raised, and they were standing on one foot. So they treated them roughly and not in accordance with the Rules of Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you see those persons being beaten?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No, the persons were not beaten. Sivac was there present, so he can testify too whether he was beaten. I couldn't see everything, but I saw a part of it, and I didn't see them being beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you see Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Kvocka was coming up. He was walking around the compound, and he saw Mr. Nusret Sivac, and he came up to him and asked, "What are you, Mr. Sivac, doing here?" And he just said that he had been taken into custody and he didn't know the reason why.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kvocka respond in any way or react to the way in which these persons were being searched?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How did he react?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka said, "Boys, that's not the way to do it. That is not how you search persons. That is not the proper way to do it. That is a very rough treatment you're giving them."

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did Kvocka come up alone or was anyone else present when he came up to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: There was another guy, a tall man with a short haircut. He was wearing the same uniform as that special unit from Banja Luka. He came up, and when Kvocka said this, he stopped the others from continuing in the same manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: The person you described as being a member of the special unit, what kind of build was he? Could you describe him?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: He was slim, with a short haircut.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: And his height?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: He was about 180 centimetres tall.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How did he stop this very rough and humiliating search?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: He told his men to stop acting in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did they obey him?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What did Kvocka do then?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka took that piece of paper from the reserve police officer, and he said that he would go up to see the bosses, to see what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did he go?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: After Mr. Kvocka left, was this search or mistreatment or humiliation of the persons taken into custody continued in any way?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How long did Mr. Kvocka spend in the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Very briefly. Maybe about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did he come back to where you were?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What did he say then?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: He said that it was a mistake with respect to Nusret Sivac, that it was his sister (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did he say anything as to what should be done with him?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said that Mr. Nusret Sivac should be taken back to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did he say that this was what the bosses had said or that he had decided so?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: He said that the bosses had said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: On that occasion, did he mention the names of those bosses or chiefs?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly. He may have mentioned them, but I was in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you mentioned the person from the reserve police force who took over the piece of paper from Tomo Stojakovic and then handed it over to Mr. Kvocka, do you know who that person was?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No. I saw him for the first time in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you went to Omarska, and you said you went there twice, did you ever enter the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where did your assignment end?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: My assignment was over once the person we were transporting got off. We then returned to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Together with Mr. Stojakovic and this other person whose name escapes me, did you take Mr. Nusret Sivac back to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Let me now ask you a few things linked to Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, excuse me. How much more time, roughly, do you need to finish the examination-in-chief? It is ten past one, so it's time for the break. I just wanted to know whether we can finish before the break or not. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Another ten minutes or so, but as it's a new area, perhaps it would be best to have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In that case, we should have the break. So we're going to have a 50-minute break. So we'll be coming back about 2.00. I'm going to ask the usher to accompany the witness out, please, and we're going to have our lunch break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, we meet again at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Would the usher have the witness introduced into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Mr. Simic, please proceed with your witness. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, you said that in 1992 you worked in the department of the Police Station Kozarac. The Prijedor Police Station, and I am talking about the basic unit, did it have any other departments?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes, it did. It had two other departments: the Omarska and Ljubija Police Departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: As a policeman yourself, did you know Mr. Kvocka because he worked in the Omarska Police Department?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know - and if so, please tell the Trial Chamber - what his status was? What were his assignments? What were his job assignments within the police system?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka was the leader of the patrol sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kvocka, in the police force system, ever have the status of the commander/commandeer of the police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Assistant commander?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Kvocka worked as the leader of the patrol sector in the Omarska Police Department. Were there any changes in respect to his employment and work post during 1992, in that sense?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was he transferred to another station in the course of 1992 at all?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes, he was transferred to the Prijedor Police Station and the reserve station at Tukovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: After Tukovi, did he return to the Omarska Police Department?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: After working in the reserve police station at Tukovi, do you know which work Mr. Kvocka performed in the Police Station of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: He was the leader of the patrol sector there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did he have the same assignments as those he had in the Police Department of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes, they were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did the leaders of patrol sectors also have the obligation and duty to do shift work on the basis of schedules?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You said that, along with this service, you too did shift work.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes. I was the junior shift officer in the Prijedor Police Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, in addition to his work as the leader of the patrol sector, did he do shift duty as well, according to the schedules of the commander of the police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes, I think he did. In 1994 and 1995, he was shift leader, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: But what about 1992? Did he do it in the same way that you and the other policemen did?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: In 1992, he was the leader of the patrol sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that Mr. Kvocka became, that is, was shift leader in 1994 and 1995, did work of that kind.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Before that, before becoming shift leader at that time, were there any changes at the head of the police force? Did you get a new police chief, and if so, who was it?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes, there was reorganisation and transformation within the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did Mr. Drljaca leave Prijedor as chief of the SJB? Did he leave and did a new chief arrive?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes, he did leave, and a new chief did arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes. It was Bogdan Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was Mr. Bogdan Delic by profession?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: He was a teacher. I think he taught. He was a teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: With the arrival of Mr. Delic, did the relationship change towards Mr. Kvocka as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Well, he went on doing the same work he had done beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who suggested that he be shift leader?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: When all our work was reorganised, the Minister made decisions with respect to the work of the police force. So the Minister or his deputy or anybody he authorised.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who made proposals to the Minister as to who ought to be put in which position?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Well, from the commander and the chief of the Public Security Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did Mr. Delic propose Mr. Kvocka as shift leader to the Minister of that department?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know, but I think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, to wind up, you worked with Mr. Kvocka for a long time. In his work, in the way he worked and functioned, did he ever show any kind of extreme nationalistic sentiments, any hatred towards the members of other nations or ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No, he did not. I have known him for many, many years, and I can say that I don't think he was a man of that kind, nor was he a policeman like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In his private life, did he socialise with Muslim policemen? Did he take them for picnics and excursions at his own holiday home at Kozara? Do you happen to know?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Finally, as a man, a personality, was he courageous, brave?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I know that he was intelligent, brave, courageous, decisive, a true professional in the line of work he did. He was not prone to drink. He was a family man. He loved his family above all else. He was a dedicated man.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kvocka frequent cafes?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Well, he went to cafes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of him going to the Stara Kuglana or Old Bowling Alley?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I don't know. I have not heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bolta. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. That completes my examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do the other Defence teams have any questions for this witness? I see that Mr. Nikolic is indicating that they do not. Very well. Mr. Bolta, you will now be answering questions put to you by the Prosecution, and I think the questions will be posed by Mr. Saxon. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, first of all, I'd simply like to clarify a few things that were not quite clear to me during your direct testimony. Early on in your testimony, you said that when you graduated from school as a police officer you first worked in Zagreb, but then you said you first worked in Pula, and those are two different places. I'm wondering if you can clarify that, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I attended a course in Pula which lasted for one year, and after I graduated from that course, I got a job in Zagreb working as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then subsequent to that, you transferred to Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And subsequent to that, you were transferred to the town of Kozarac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who requested your transfer from Prijedor to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: The commander of the police station of Prijedor, Esad Alic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So was it a simple administrative transfer?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Well, yes. Every commander can transfer policemen where he considers they would be used best.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Kozarac is a small community, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I think you explained that at least in 1992, at that time there were nine policemen and a commander of the police department there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Before 1992, when I was transferred, there were nine policeman and the commander was the tenth, but when the nationalistic feelings began, then there were a lot of reserve policemen working in Kozarac in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Prior to 1992, there was no deputy commander, was there?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No. Afterwards, the police department did not have a deputy or an assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, Omarska as well, the police department in Omarska, that was a very small police department, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It had a commander but no deputy commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How about the police station in Prijedor, in the town of Prijedor itself? Approximately how many policemen worked in that police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I think about 60 policemen. I don't know the exact number, but it would be thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That police station had a commander and a deputy commander, did it not, at least prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So if there was an even larger police unit involving about 90 police officers, would that unit also possibly have a commander and a deputy commander? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness, this one and the previous one, said quite definitely that the law regulated that the police station had a hierarchy, that a department had its hierarchy, and I don't see where this line of questioning is leading by my learned colleague, asking the witness to explain a department. How could a department have something that was not in line with the law? Because the witness said that everything was regulated by law. So I don't see the point of asking witnesses this type of question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, what is the purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the point of my question goes to the possibility of Article 7(3) responsibility in this case, and when the police structures in the Prijedor area at that time felt the need to have not only a commander but also deputy commanders, perhaps other commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we come back to the same thing. A department, a police station, all that is regulated by law. Somebody has prescribed that a department exists, unless the law is changed, is amended. And then the fact that a lot of work security-wise came about, that somebody could decide otherwise, let's especially not have this witness speak about that, because it was strictly regulated by rules and the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we are here to establish the facts. So in order to arrive at the facts, ask your questions, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, if a police structure organisation involving about 90 police officers were created, would it then be likely, or possible at least, that there would be not only a commander but a deputy commander, at least prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I think there was a deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Could I just make one small intervention on that because I was getting myself -- it seems to me he's not an expert witness; therefore, his opinion or hypotheticals dealing with the structure, it may be -- but as a policeman in the area, it may be - I don't know - that he knows what the biggest police station was and how many policemen it had and whether they had commanders or deputies. That would be a matter of his factual knowledge. But a matter of his opinion, I have a little trouble with too, since he's a fact witness and not an opinion witness. I just throw that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, what was the largest police station in the Banja Luka/Prijedor area prior to 1992, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: The largest police station, is that what you want to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In terms of numbers of police officers working there.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Well, Banja Luka was bigger, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Approximately, if you know, how many police officers worked at the Banja Luka Police Station?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know if the Banja Luka Police Station had a commander and a deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Well, according to the law, it must have had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bolta, did you support the separation of your police structure from the central government in Sarajevo in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Well, I didn't understand that question. Could you repeat your question, please? I don't follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, prior to the outbreak of the armed conflict, the police structure that you worked for reported eventually to the Ministry in Sarajevo, did it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In late April 1992, Serb forces took over the town of Prijedor, did they not?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: After that time, your police force no longer responded in the chain of command to the former Ministry in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question, simply, then, is: Did you support that separation of your police structure out of the former police structure that existed?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No. I was an ordinary policeman. It wasn't mine to think about things like that, up to me; it wasn't up to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to your testimony regarding the detention camps that you said you were aware existed in Prijedor. You said that it was known amongst the police officers in Prijedor that these detention camps existed. How was this fact known? How did it become known to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Well, people were taken off there, they were taken away. People would come to the police station and ask, and we sent them to the Omarska Police Station to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say that "people were taken off there," are you referring to Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, regarding the first time you visited Omarska in 1992 - I believe you said it was between the 8th and the 12th of June, 1992 - can you tell us who ordered you to transport those prisoners to Omarska that day?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I received an order from the shift leader, and the shift leader gets orders from his superiors. Now, I don't know who that was exactly, but via the shift leader, work was coordinated further down the line, reaching us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was the name of the shift leader who gave you that order between the 8th and the 12th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: His name was Ratko Gvozden.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I ask you: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, on that day when you made that first trip to Omarska, what was the temperature like?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Well, the temperature was around 20 to 25 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were the windows open in the van? I'm talking about in the area where the prisoners were.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that you -- one of the persons that you transported that day was Mr. Nusret Sivac. Do you know his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I think he was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You also mentioned that there were two other prisoners in the back of that van with Nusret Sivac. Can you please give us the names of those two other prisoners who were in the back of the van when you set out from the Prijedor Police Station?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, would the name Omer Kerenovic mean anything to you? A former judge.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No, I don't know that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How about the name Safet Ramadanovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No, I don't know that man either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know where these men were from?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Keraterm camp, because, as you explained, that was your first stop, do you recall seeing Mr. Zoran Zigic there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, you're going to have an opportunity to redirect afterwards, if that was what you wanted, but let's hear the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We do consider that this question should not be allowed in the cross in view of the examination-in-chief that went before it. Zoran Zigic was not mentioned, nor any event concerning him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, we know that. We know that Mr. Zigic was not mentioned, but we also know the rest of it, and so do you. You are well aware of what we accorded earlier on. Is that what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let's have the question, and you'll have time to question the witness as well in your turn. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question was: When you first arrived at the Keraterm camp, do you recall seeing Mr. Zoran Zigic there?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Zoran Zigic from before the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know him well, just -- I don't actually know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you know Zoran Zigic by sight? Did you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I knew that he was a taxi driver for a time. What else he did, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is going a little too far and is becoming testimony regarding Mr. Zigic. If we touched upon Keraterm and said that he did not see Zoran Zigic there, I don't think we should go any further. But I also agree with you that there is some connection, but as he already said, he didn't see him in Keraterm. Perhaps he could ask about Omarska, but that would be that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon. Could you explain the objective of your question, please, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The objective, Your Honour, is -- the next question I was going to put to this witness was whether he could recall the accused I just mentioned and another man assaulting one of the prisoners in -- that was in the van that was being driven or accompanied by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, the van -- I believe you were driving the van. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When your van stopped at Keraterm, do you recall two persons dragging one of the prisoners out of the back of your van and beginning to beat them? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness never mentioned that he ever got out of the van, and especially not that anyone was beaten, and perhaps questions can be asked as to whether the witness had ever gone out of the van or whether he had seen anything, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. Mr. Saxon, please ask him whether or not he ever got out of the van. That is the way in which you should rephrase the question, and you can well do it. So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At Keraterm, Mr. Bolta, did you ever step out of the van?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At any time while you were in Keraterm, did anyone remove any of the prisoners from that van and begin to beat them?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were there prisoners from Keraterm placed in your van at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Yes. They had already been prepared and had already entered the van.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: As those prisoners were entering the van, could you see what was happening to them?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No. I was behind the wheel, and my colleague, who was in charge, Tomo Stojakovic, just closed the door. The people entered, and we went on to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any screams or cries of pain at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: No. There was nothing of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever turn around to look at the prisoners from Keraterm who were placed in that van that you were driving?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: I couldn't have seen them because I look in front of me when I'm driving.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before you drove away from Keraterm, did you ever turn around and look at the prisoners that had been placed in the van at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA
utterances.text: Well, no. The people were already prepared when I had entered the front part of the vehicle and they entered in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
